A mechanical mixing valve provides reliable temperature control using a passive thermostatic element, without the need for electronic controls, sensors, or external power.

This retrofit would simplify DHW system operation, reduce long-term maintenance costs, and improve serviceability. Mechanical mixing valves can typically be adjusted, repaired, or replaced by building maintenance staff, reducing reliance on specialized service providers. 

*Further engineering review would be required to confirm valve sizing, temperature setpoints, and compatibility with the existing DHW storage and distribution system.
measures.summary: Replace existing Flowmix electric mixging valve with mechanical mixing valve when the unit end of its life. The proposed valve would maintain consistent and safe DHW delivery temperatures while improving system robustness and long-term maintainability.

measures.title: MUA Retrofit Two (2) Option: Hydronic MUA with VFD / WSHP MUA with VFD
measures.existing: Ventilation for the building is provided by One (1) make-up air (MUA) units, located in roof top, serving corridors and other public areas. During the site visit it was unable to access to roof top, report by on site staff the units are original to the building, installed in 1998, and have exceeded their expected service life
measures.retrofit:
Option 1 – Install VFDs and Convert existing MUA to Hydronic MUA
Mann recommends installing a new hydronic heating coil in the existing make-up air (MUA) unit, to be served by the central boiler plant. A modulating control valve would regulate heating-water flow to maintain corridor supply-air temperature. (Where applicable, the existing heating and/or cooling coils may be able to be retained or reused, subject to condition verification.)
As the existing MUA unit is currently operating without VFD control, new variable-frequency drives (VFDs) should be installed on the supply fan to enable proper airflow modulation. Once installed, the VFDs will be fully integrated into the BAS to provide optimized fan control, scheduling, and occupancy-based ventilation reduction.
Hydronic conversion also reduces maintenance requirements and qualifies for Enbridge incentives, improving overall project payback.
Option 2 – Install VFDs and Convert existing MUA to Water-Source Heat Pump (WSHP) MUA
Mann recommends converting the existing make-up air (MUA) unit to a water-source heat pump (WSHP) MUA unit. The new WSHP heating coil can be installed within the existing MUA cabinet, allowing the building to retain most of the original ventilation infrastructure.
Because the building already has a WSHP loop, the conversion is simpler and more cost effective. 
A WSHP system is significantly more efficient than a gas fired burner because it uses the thermal energy already present within the building—rather than generating heat through combustion. The WSHP coil is capable of providing heating whenever the ventilation system operates and can take advantage of heat already present in the hydronic loop, reducing boiler runtime and improving overall system efficiency. One consideration is that the MUA electrical load may increase slightly depending on the WSHP coil configuration; however, the improved efficiency and reduced gas usage often outweigh these impacts.
During the heating season, the WSHP coil extracts heat from the hydronic loop and transfers it into the ventilation air stream. When more heat is required than is being generated within the building, the central boiler plant provides supplemental heat to maintain loop temperature.
During warmer weather, suites operating in cooling mode can reject heat into the WSHP loop, supplying “free heat” to the MUA heating coil during mild outdoor conditions. During shoulder seasons, the system can recycle heat internally: heat removed from south-facing suites in cooling mode can offset ventilation heating demands from north-facing corridors, reducing the need for gas-fired heating entirely.
*Where applicable, IESO incentives and Enbridge incentives for central heating system efficiency upgrades may be available and could help improve overall project economics. Additional information regarding current incentive programs can be found on Mann Engineering’s website:
https://www.mannengineering.com/100-000-enbridge-incentive
measures.summary: Upgrade the existing MUA system by adding VFD control and converting to either a hydronic or water-source heat pump configuration to improve energy efficiency. Qualify for Enbridge incentives.

measures.title: Primary–Secondary Boiler and Hydronic Loop Reconfiguration (Primary loop + WSHP loop + DHW loop)
measures.existing: The existing piping arrangement separates the WSHP loop, primary heating loop, and domestic hot water (DHW) loop into independent hydronic systems, each served by dedicated boilers and pumping configurations. The primary heating loop operates at higher temperatures for space heating, the WSHP loop operates at lower temperatures, and the DHW system functions on a separate loop without hydraulic or control integration. This configuration increases system complexity and limits opportunities for load diversity, heat recovery, and coordinated temperature optimization. During shoulder seasons, independent loop operation can contribute to boiler short cycling, elevated supply temperatures, and reduced overall plant efficiency.
measures.retrofit:
It is recommended to evaluate reconfiguring the WSHP loop, primary heating loop, and DHW piping into a coordinated Primary–Secondary (P-S) hydronic arrangement. Under a P-S configuration, a central boiler primary loop would maintain controlled supply temperatures while secondary loops draw only the required flow and temperature for each load. This arrangement provides hydraulic separation, allows differentiated temperature control for high- and low-temperature systems, improves outdoor-air reset effectiveness, and reduces short cycling. Improved integration may also enhance return-water temperature control, supporting more efficient boiler operation. When implemented in conjunction with condensing boiler upgrades, this redesign may allow optimization of boiler staging and potential reduction in total boiler count, thereby lowering long-term maintenance complexity and operating costs. Further engineering review is required to confirm detailed hydraulic configuration, load diversity assumptions, and control sequencing strategy.
*Where applicable, IESO incentives and Enbridge incentives for central heating system efficiency upgrades may be available and could help improve overall project economics.
Additional information regarding current incentive programs can be found on Mann Engineering’s website:
https://www.mannengineering.com/100-000-enbridge-incentive
measures.summary: Reconfigure Primary heating loop, WSHP loop and DHW loop to a primary–secondary layout, hydraulically separating loops to improve temperature control, boiler protection and plant efficiency.

measures.title: Install Motorized Damper for Garage Air Intake
measures.existing: The parking garage air intake is not equipped with a motorized damper. Outdoor air enters the space continuously, which can result in excessive cold air infiltration during winter conditions. This may contribute to lower garage temperatures, increased heating demand where applicable, and reduced occupant comfort near entry points. No active control strategy was observed to regulate intake airflow based on outdoor temperature or operating conditions.
measures.retrofit: It is recommended to install a motorized damper at the garage outdoor air intake, integrated with a temperature sensor and control logic to modulate airflow based on outdoor conditions. The damper would reduce unnecessary cold air infiltration during winter while maintaining required ventilation rates. Integration with the existing garage fan controls or BAS (where available) would allow coordinated operation and improved seasonal performance. This measure would help stabilize garage temperatures, reduce potential heating energy demand, and improve occupant comfort near entry areas
measures.summary: Install a motorized intake damper to reduce winter cold air infiltration and improve garage temperature control while maintaining required ventilation.

measures.title: Convert In-Suite PTAC to Air-Source Heat Pump System
measures.existing:
Heating and cooling within individual suites are currently provided by in-suite PTAC units consisting of electric resistance radiators for space heating and an integral DX cooling coil for space cooling. Each unit operates independently and is controlled by a local thermostat.

Electric resistance heating operates with a coefficient of performance (COP) of approximately 1.0, meaning that electrical energy is converted directly into heat without efficiency amplification. The DX cooling section typically achieves cooling COP values in the range of 2.8–3.5, depending on age and maintenance condition.

While this decentralized configuration provides simple suite-level control, it results in relatively high electrical consumption during the heating season and ongoing maintenance requirements, including heating element replacement, compressor servicing, condensate management, and periodic fan motor repairs. As these units age, performance declines and lifecycle costs increase. In addition, the distributed nature of the equipment limits opportunities for centralized optimization and coordinated energy management.
measures.retrofit:
Mann recommends replacing the existing electric radiator + DX PTAC units with modern air-source heat pump (ASHP) systems. ASHP systems provide both heating and cooling through a high-efficiency refrigeration cycle and eliminate the need for electric resistance heating.

Modern cold-climate ASHP systems can achieve heating and cooling COP values exceeding 4.0–5.0 under favorable conditions, significantly improving energy efficiency compared to electric resistance heating and conventional DX configurations. In addition, improved part-load modulation enhances occupant comfort and reduces peak electrical demand.

The proposed retrofit would improve suite-level temperature control, reduce long-term maintenance costs, and align the building with electrification and decarbonization strategies. Phased implementation may be considered to align with reserve fund planning and suite turnover cycles.

*Where applicable, IESO incentives and Enbridge incentives for central heating system efficiency upgrades may be available and could help improve overall project economics. Additional information regarding current incentive programs can be found on Mann Engineering’s website:
https://www.mannengineering.com/100-000-enbridge-incentive

*This measure is recommended subject to a detailed feasibility study to be carried out at the next project stage or as part of an ASHRAE Level 2 Energy Audit. The feasibility assessment should consider the available electrical service capacity, potential electrical infrastructure upgrades, and system integration constraints. It is also recommended that the existing hydronic heating system be retained as a backup system to ensure reliability and operational flexibility.
measures.summary: Replace in-suite PTAC units with high-efficiency air-source heat pump systems to improve energy performance, reduce maintenance costs, and support long-term building electrification.

measures.title: Convert In-Suite Electric Water Heaters to Heat Pump Water Heaters (HPWH)
measures.existing:
DHW for each suite is served by an individual electric storage-type water heater, typically rated at approximately 3,000 W. These units operate independently and provide hot water directly to each dwelling unit.

Electric resistance water heaters convert electricity directly into heat and operate with a coefficient of performance (COP) of approximately 1.0. While this decentralized configuration simplifies distribution and eliminates centralized piping losses, it results in relatively high electrical consumption compared to centralized condensing or heat pump–based systems.

Conversion to a centralized domestic hot water system or the implementation of heat pump water heaters (HPWH) may offer improved energy performance and reduced electrical consumption. However, such an upgrade would require a detailed feasibility assessment, including evaluation of available electrical capacity, spatial constraints, ventilation requirements, and capital cost implications.

Accordingly, further review as part of an ASHRAE Level 2 Energy Audit or dedicated heat pump feasibility study is recommended to determine the technical and economic viability of transitioning to a heat pump–based DHW solution.
measures.retrofit:
Mann recommends replacing the existing in-suite electric resistance storage water heaters with high-efficiency heat pump water heaters (HPWH). Heat pump water heaters extract heat from ambient air and transfer it to domestic water, typically achieving COP values in the range of 2.5–4.0, significantly reducing electrical consumption compared to resistance-based systems (COP ≈ 1.0).

This approach maintains the existing decentralized configuration and avoids the substantial capital cost associated with installing a centralized DHW plant, including new boilers, distribution piping, and major mechanical room reconfiguration. Implementation would require review of available electrical capacity, ventilation and air-source requirements, condensate drainage provisions, and space constraints within each suite or mechanical area.

*Where applicable, IESO incentives and Enbridge incentives for central heating system efficiency upgrades may be available and could help improve overall project economics. Additional information regarding current incentive programs can be found on Mann Engineering’s website:
https://www.mannengineering.com/100-000-enbridge-incentive

*This measure is recommended subject to a detailed feasibility study to be carried out at the next project stage or as part of an ASHRAE Level 2 Energy Audit. The feasibility assessment should consider the available electrical service capacity, potential electrical infrastructure upgrades, and system integration constraints. It is also recommended that the existing hydronic heating system be retained as a backup system to ensure reliability and operational flexibility.
measures.summary: Replace electric water heaters with heat pump water heaters to significantly reduce electricity consumption.

measures.title: Retrofit Existing MUA to ASHP-Based MUA with VFD (Gas Heating as Backup)
measures.existing: The building is served by a make-up air (MUA) unit equipped with a gas-fired heating section and fixed or limited-speed supply fan control. The unit provides ventilation air to corridors and common areas but relies primarily on natural gas combustion for winter heating. While the system is functional, gas-fired heating results in ongoing fuel consumption and limits opportunities for electrification and high-efficiency operation.
measures.retrofit:
Mann recommends retrofitting the existing MUA unit to operate as an air-source heat pump (ASHP)–based MUA system while retaining the existing gas-fired heating section as a backup for extreme cold-weather conditions. Under the proposed configuration, an ASHP heating and cooling section would be integrated into the existing MUA cabinet (subject to engineering review), allowing the unit to provide high-efficiency heating and cooling through a refrigeration cycle.

New or upgraded variable frequency drives (VFDs) would be installed on the supply fan to enable airflow modulation based on ventilation demand and discharge air temperature requirements. Integration into a Building Automation System (BAS), where available, would allow optimized scheduling, temperature reset, and coordinated system control.

The ASHP system would handle the majority of annual heating and cooling loads, significantly reducing natural gas consumption, while the existing gas-fired section would operate only as supplemental or emergency heat. This hybrid approach improves energy efficiency, supports decarbonization goals, and minimizes capital cost by retaining functional components of the existing unit.

*This measure is recommended subject to a detailed feasibility study to confirm equipment sizing, electrical service capacity, structural considerations, and integration constraints. The existing gas-fired heating section is recommended to be retained as backup to ensure reliability and operational flexibility.

*Where applicable, IESO and Enbridge incentives for heating system efficiency upgrades may be available and could help improve overall project economics. Additional information regarding current incentive programs can be found on Mann Engineering’s website:
https://www.mannengineering.com/100-000-enbridge-incentive
measures.summary: Upgrade the MUA to a heat pump–based system with VFD control while retaining gas heating as backup to reduce gas use and improve energy performance.

measures.title: Suite Pump VFD Retrofit
measures.existing: Suite-level hydronic circulation pumps are currently operating at constant speed to deliver heating or cooling water to fan coil units. Flow is typically balanced using manual balancing valves or fixed control settings. As a result, the pumps operate at full speed regardless of actual thermal demand, leading to unnecessary energy consumption and increased mechanical wear during periods of partial load.
measures.retrofit: It is recommended to install variable frequency drives (VFDs) on the suite-level circulation pumps to allow pump speed to modulate based on real-time demand. The VFD would adjust pump output in response to pressure differential or control valve position, enabling reduced flow during low-load conditions. This retrofit reduces electrical energy consumption, extends pump life, and improves hydronic system stability while maintaining adequate heating and cooling performance. Further engineering is required to confirm control strategy, sensor placement, and system compatibility.
measures.summary: Convert constant-speed suite circulation pumps to VFD control to match flow with demand and reduce pump energy consumption.
